slides.narration: Why does a heavy almirah refuse to move when you push gently, then suddenly slide once you push harder? Why is it easier to keep it sliding than to start it? In this part we look at what friction really is at the surface, how it adjusts itself, and the laws and graph that describe it.

slides.heading: What is friction?
slides.body_md: **Friction** is the force that opposes the relative motion, or the tendency of relative motion, between two surfaces in contact. It acts **along** the surfaces.
bullets: We meet four kinds: static, limiting, kinetic (sliding) and rolling friction.
Friction is useful in walking, braking and holding a nail, and harmful in wearing out machine parts and wasting energy as heat.
It is a contact force, so it always comes together with a normal reaction $N$ from the same surface.

rows: Acts between surfaces at rest relative to each other; adjusts itself up to a maximum
A scooter parked on a slope
The greatest static friction, just before sliding begins
The push at which a loaded trolley just starts to move
Acts between surfaces sliding over each other; nearly constant, less than limiting friction
A brick sliding down a plank
Acts on a wheel or ball rolling without slipping; much the smallest
A cricket ball rolling over the outfield

slides.narration: Friction is the force that opposes the sliding, or the attempt to slide, of one surface over another. It acts along the surfaces. We shall meet four kinds: static, limiting, kinetic and rolling. Friction helps us walk and stop a vehicle, but it also wears out machines and turns useful energy into heat. It always comes together with the normal reaction of the same surface.

slides.heading: Classical view: interlocking
slides.body_md: Even a polished surface is rough when magnified. The **classical view** says friction arises because the hills of one surface **interlock** with the hollows of the other.
bullets: To slide, one surface must be lifted over the hills of the other, or the hills must be sheared off.
Pressing the surfaces together meshes the hills more deeply, so more force is needed: friction grows with $N$.
The view explains why rough surfaces grip well, but it fails for very smooth, clean surfaces.

slides.narration: Under a microscope even a polished surface looks like a range of hills and hollows. The classical view says that friction comes from these hills fitting into the hollows of the other surface. To slide, the hills must be lifted over each other or broken off. Pressing harder makes them mesh deeper, so friction grows with the normal reaction. But the view fails for very smooth surfaces.

slides.heading: Modern view: adhesion and cold welding
slides.body_md: The surfaces touch only at the **tips of the highest hills**, so the real area of contact is a tiny fraction of the apparent area.
bullets: At these tips the pressure is enormous: the atoms of the two surfaces come within atomic range and **stick**, a process called **cold welding** (adhesion).
Sliding means breaking these junctions again and again; **friction is the force needed to shear them**.
A larger $N$ flattens more tips, so the real contact area grows in proportion to $N$. That is why friction is proportional to $N$ and nearly independent of the apparent area.
Highly polished, clean surfaces can stick **more**, which the classical view cannot explain.

slides.narration: The modern view says the surfaces really touch only at the tips of the highest hills. There the pressure is so large that the atoms of the two surfaces stick together, which is called cold welding. Friction is the force needed to break these tiny welds. More pressing flattens more tips, so the real contact grows in proportion to the normal reaction, and that explains the proportionality.

slides.heading: Static friction is self-adjusting
slides.body_md: When a body is at rest and a force $F$ tries to move it, **static friction** $f_s$ appears and is equal and opposite to $F$, whatever $F$ is, up to a limit.
bullets: $F = 0$: friction is zero. Push with $60$ N: friction is $60$ N. Push with $120$ N: friction is $120$ N. The body stays at rest because the two forces balance.
Static friction **adjusts itself** to the applied force; it is **not** fixed at $\mu_s N$.
The adjustment stops at a maximum value, the **limiting friction** $f_{\max}$. For this crate it is $154.3$ N.
Beyond that the junctions break, the crate slides and friction falls to the kinetic value $102.9$ N.

With one hundred and twenty, friction is one hundred and twenty. Static friction adjusts itself to match the push, so the crate stays at rest. This continues up to a maximum, the limiting friction, one hundred and fifty four point three newtons here. Beyond it the crate slides.

slides.heading: Limiting, kinetic friction and the coefficients
slides.body_md: The ratios of friction to the normal reaction are constants for a given pair of surfaces. They are **pure numbers** (no unit).
bullets: Hence $f_{\max} = \mu_s N$ and $f_k = \mu_k N$. For any pair of surfaces $\mu_k < \mu_s$: it is easier to keep a body sliding than to start it.
The inequality $f_s \le \mu_s N$ holds while the body is at rest; the equality holds **only at the point of sliding**.
Coefficients can exceed 1 for very sticky pairs such as rubber on dry concrete.

visual.alt: Table of limiting friction, coefficient of static friction, kinetic friction and coefficient of kinetic friction with the values for a 35 kilogram crate

slides.narration: The coefficient of static friction is the limiting friction divided by the normal reaction. The coefficient of kinetic friction is the sliding friction divided by the normal reaction. Both are pure numbers, and the kinetic one is smaller. So the limiting friction is mu s times N, and the kinetic friction is mu k times N. The equality for static friction holds only at the instant before sliding begins.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: pushing a crate
slides.body_md: A crate of mass $35$ kg stands on a floor with $\mu_s = 0.45$ and $\mu_k = 0.3$. Taking $g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$, find the friction when it is pushed horizontally with (i) $60$ N, (ii) $180$ N, and the acceleration in case (ii).
bullets: (i) $60$ N is below the limit: the crate stays at rest and $f_s = 60$ N.
(ii) $180$ N exceeds $154.3$ N: the crate slides, $f_k = \mu_k N = 0.3 \times 343.0 = 102.9$ N.

visual.caption: Static friction adjusts itself; kinetic friction is smaller and steady.

slides.narration: The normal reaction is thirty five times nine point eight, which is three hundred and forty three newtons. The limiting friction is zero point four five times that, one hundred and fifty four point three newtons. A push of sixty newtons is below it, so the friction is sixty newtons and nothing moves. A push of one hundred and eighty newtons is above it, so the crate slides, with kinetic friction one hundred and two point nine newtons. The acceleration is two point two metres per second squared.

slides.heading: The graph of friction against applied force
slides.body_md: Increase the applied force $F$ slowly from zero and plot the friction $f$.
bullets: **Static part** (a straight line of slope 1): $f = F$, as the crate stays at rest, up to the peak at $f_{\max} = 154.3$ N.
**The drop:** the instant sliding starts, friction falls from $f_{\max}$ to $f_k = 102.9$ N, because $\mu_k < \mu_s$.
**Kinetic part:** a nearly horizontal line: kinetic friction does not change much with the applied force or the speed.
Beyond the peak the net force $F - f_k$ is not zero, so the body accelerates.

visual.alt: Friction against applied force for a 35 kilogram crate: friction rises along the line f equals F up to the limiting value of 154.4 newtons, then drops to the constant kinetic value of 102.9 newtons once the crate slides
visual.caption: Static friction adjusts to the push up to the limit; kinetic friction is smaller and steady.

slides.narration: Here is the graph. For small pushes the friction rises along a straight line at forty five degrees, because friction equals the push. The line ends at a peak, the limiting friction. At that point the body starts to slide, and the friction drops to the smaller kinetic value. After that the line is almost flat, because kinetic friction hardly depends on the applied force.

slides.narration: What happens to the friction at the instant sliding starts?

slides.heading: Rolling friction
slides.body_md: **Rolling friction** opposes the motion of a wheel or ball that rolls without slipping. It is **much smaller** than sliding friction.
bullets: The point of the wheel touching the ground is momentarily at rest, so there is no sliding and no junctions are being sheared; the loss comes mainly from the slight flattening of wheel and road, and each flattening is quickly undone.
In order of size: $\text{rolling} < \text{kinetic} < \text{limiting static}$.
This is why we put heavy loads on wheels, and why a ball bearing beats a sliding bearing.

rows: Steel wheel rolling on steel rail

visual.alt: Table of typical approximate coefficients of static and kinetic friction for four pairs of surfaces and the much smaller rolling value for a steel wheel on a rail

slides.narration: Rolling friction acts on a wheel or ball that rolls without slipping. It is much smaller than sliding friction, because the part of the wheel touching the ground is momentarily at rest, so no junctions are torn apart, and the small losses come from the slight flattening of the wheel and the road. In order of size, rolling friction is least, then kinetic, then limiting static friction.

slides.heading: Laws of friction
slides.body_md: Experiments on blocks, spring balances and inclined planes give these laws, which hold well for ordinary dry surfaces.
bullets: Doubling the load on a block doubles $N$, and therefore doubles both $f_{\max}$ and $f_k$.
Turning a brick from its broad face to its narrow face leaves $f_{\max}$ unchanged: the real contact area depends on $N$, not on the apparent area.
The laws are approximate: they fail at very high speeds, very high pressures and for very smooth surfaces.

rows: Friction acts along the surfaces in contact, opposite to the relative motion or its tendency
Limiting friction is proportional to the normal reaction: f(max) = μs N
Limiting friction does not depend on the apparent area of contact
It depends on the materials and roughness, through μs
fk = μk N: nearly independent of speed and area, and less than limiting friction

slides.narration: These are the laws of friction. Friction acts along the surface and opposes the motion or its tendency. Limiting friction is proportional to the normal reaction, does not depend on the apparent area of contact, and depends on the nature of the surfaces. Kinetic friction is also proportional to the normal reaction, nearly independent of speed and area, and smaller than the limiting value. The laws are approximate.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: measuring the coefficients
slides.body_md: A wooden block of mass $3.2$ kg on a horizontal board just starts to slide when the spring balance reads $12.5$ N, and keeps moving at constant speed at $9.4$ N. Find $\mu_s$ and $\mu_k$. If a load of $2$ kg is placed on the block, what is the new limiting friction? ($g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$.)
bullets: With the load, $N = 5.2 \times 9.8 = 50.96$ N.
New limiting friction $= \mu_s N = 0.399 \times 50.96 = 20.3$ N: it grows in the ratio of the normal reactions.

rows: Normal reaction with the extra load

visual.alt: Table of the working for measuring the coefficients of friction of a wooden block: normal reaction, coefficient of static friction, predicted limiting friction with a load and coefficient of kinetic friction

slides.narration: The normal reaction is three point two times nine point eight, about thirty one point three six newtons. The static coefficient is twelve point five over that, about zero point three nine nine, and the kinetic coefficient is nine point four over that, about zero point three. Adding two kilograms raises the normal reaction to fifty point nine six newtons, so the limiting friction rises to twenty point three newtons.

slides.heading: Friction is a non-conservative force
slides.body_md: A force is **conservative** if the work it does between two points is the same along every path, so the work around a closed path is zero. Friction fails this test.
bullets: Kinetic friction has the fixed magnitude $\mu_k N$ and **always opposes the displacement**, so the work it does is $-\mu_k N \times (\text{path length})$: it **grows with the path**.
The work around a closed path is **not zero**: it is negative, however the body returns.
So no potential energy can be defined for friction. The mechanical energy lost is changed into **heat** at the surfaces.
Gravity, by contrast, is conservative: the work depends only on the end points.

A to B round the corner (6 m then 8 m)
A to B and back by the straight line

visual.alt: Table of the work done against friction on a 20 kilogram box between two points: straight path, path round a corner and the round trip

slides.narration: A conservative force does the same work between two points along any path, and zero work around a closed path. Friction does not. Kinetic friction always opposes the motion, so the work it does is minus its magnitude times the length of the path travelled. A longer path means more work. Around a closed loop the work is not zero, so friction has no potential energy; the lost energy becomes heat.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: two routes for a box
slides.body_md: A $20$ kg box is dragged slowly over a rough floor from A to B ($\mu_k = 0.25$, $g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$). Find the work done against friction along (i) the straight $10$ m path, (ii) the path round a corner of $6$ m and $8$ m, and (iii) a round trip A to B and back by the straight path.
bullets: $f_k = \mu_k mg = 0.25 \times 20 \times 9.8 = 49.0$ N, the same on every path.
(i) $W = f_k \times 10 = 490$ J. (ii) $W = f_k \times 14 = 686$ J.
(iii) $W = f_k \times 20 = 980$ J, **not zero**: friction is non-conservative.
The box is at the same height and the same place at the start and end of (iii), yet energy has been lost as heat.

slides.narration: Kinetic friction is zero point two five times twenty times nine point eight, which is forty nine newtons, on every path. Along the straight ten metres, the work against it is four hundred and ninety joules. Round the corner, fourteen metres, it is six hundred and eighty six joules. For the round trip it is nine hundred and eighty joules, not zero. The same start and end, yet different work, so friction is non-conservative.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 1
slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: Friction from interlocking of hills and hollows
Adhesion (cold welding) at the few points of real contact
Self-adjusting: f = F while at rest, up to f(max) = μs N
fk = μk N, with μk < μs; nearly constant
Much the smallest: rolling < kinetic < limiting static
Line of slope 1 to the peak, drop, then nearly flat
Depends on the path: non-conservative; energy goes to heat

visual.alt: Summary table of the views of friction, static, kinetic and rolling friction, the friction graph and the non-conservative nature of friction

slides.narration: To sum up. Classically, friction comes from interlocking; in the modern view it comes from adhesion at the few points of real contact. Static friction adjusts itself up to the limiting value, mu s times N. Kinetic friction is mu k times N and smaller. Rolling friction is smallest. The graph rises along a straight line, drops at the peak, and then runs almost flat. Friction is non-conservative.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 1
bullets: When asked for the friction on a body **at rest**, check first whether it is below the limit: then it equals the applied force (or the balancing component), **not** $\mu_s N$.
Use $\mu_s N$ only when the body is just about to slide, and $\mu_k N$ once it is sliding.
In the graph, label the axes, the peak ($f_{\max}$), the drop and the kinetic level, and show the first part at 45°.
For the modern view write: real contact only at tips, atoms adhere (cold welding), friction is the force to break the junctions.

Common mistakes: saying friction depends on the area of contact; saying $\mu$ has a unit; saying friction always opposes **motion** (it opposes relative motion, and may help a walking person move forward).

slides.narration: How much force does it take to push a loaded trolley up a ramp? Will a box stay put on a tilted plank? Why does a gardener find it easier to pull a lawn roller than to push it? In this part we answer these questions with friction and the normal reaction, and finish with the angles of friction and repose and with ways of reducing friction.

slides.heading: Forces on a block on an incline
slides.body_md: A block of mass $m$ on a slope of angle $\theta$ is acted on by its weight $mg$ (down), the normal reaction $N$ (perpendicular to the slope) and friction (along the slope). Resolve the weight:
bullets: The normal reaction on a slope is **less than** $mg$, by the factor $\cos\theta$: do not write $N = mg$.
The angle between the weight and the perpendicular to the slope equals the slope angle $\theta$.
Friction acts **along the slope**, opposite to the motion (or its tendency).

rows: Component perpendicular to the slope (= N)
μ N = μ mg cos θ

visual.alt: Table of the weight, its component along the slope, its component perpendicular to the slope and the greatest friction for a 40 kilogram block on a 20 degree slope

math: mg\sin\theta \ \text{along the slope} \qquad mg\cos\theta \ \text{perpendicular to the slope}
slides.narration: Resolve the weight into two parts. The part m g sine theta acts along the slope, down it. The part m g cosine theta presses the block into the slope and is balanced by the normal reaction. So on a slope the normal reaction is m g cosine theta, less than the weight. The greatest friction is mu times this. Friction acts along the slope, against the motion or its tendency.

slides.heading: A block at rest on a slope
slides.body_md: While the block is at rest, static friction balances the pull of the weight down the slope: $f_s = mg\sin\theta$. It can do so only while this does not exceed the limit $\mu_s mg\cos\theta$.
bullets: Friction on a block at rest is $mg\sin\theta$, **not** $\mu_s mg\cos\theta$: it is self-adjusting, rising as the slope is tilted.
The block begins to slide when $mg\sin\theta = \mu_s mg\cos\theta$, that is $\tan\theta = \mu_s$.
The mass cancels, so heavy and light blocks slide at the same slope angle.

functions.label: mg sin θ: pull of the weight down the slope (5 kg)
μs mg cos θ: greatest friction (μs = 0.5)

visual.alt: Two curves against the slope angle for a 5 kilogram block with coefficient of static friction 0.5: the weight component down the slope rises while the greatest friction falls, and they cross at 26.6 degrees, the angle of repose
visual.caption: The block slides once mg sin θ exceeds μs mg cos θ: beyond tan θ = μs.

slides.narration: While the block stays at rest, friction exactly balances the part of the weight along the slope, m g sine theta. As you tilt the plank, this rises, as the first curve shows, while the greatest friction available falls, as the second curve shows. Where the curves cross, the block is about to slide, and there tan theta equals mu s. The mass cancels, so it does not matter how heavy the block is.

slides.heading: Sliding down a rough incline
slides.body_md: When the block slides down, kinetic friction $\mu_k N$ acts **up** the slope. Along the slope, taking down as positive:
bullets: Perpendicular to the slope there is no acceleration, so $N = mg\cos\theta$.
The mass cancels: $a$ does not depend on $m$. For a smooth slope $\mu_k = 0$ and $a = g\sin\theta$.
If $\tan\theta \le \mu_k$, the expression is zero or negative: a block already sliding slows down and stops, or slides at constant speed if $\tan\theta = \mu_k$.

slides.body_md: To push the block **up** the slope with a force $P$ along the slope, friction acts **down** the slope (against the motion):

slides.heading: Worked example 5: sliding down
slides.body_md: A $25$ kg block is released from rest on a $35^\circ$ slope ($\mu_k = 0.3$, $g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$). Find its acceleration, the time to slide $6$ m and its speed after sliding $6$ m.
bullets: Check with forces: $mg\sin\theta - \mu N = 140.5 - 60.2 = 80.3$ N, and $\dfrac{80.3}{25} = 3.213$ m s$^{-2}$.
$s = \tfrac{1}{2}at^2 \Rightarrow t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 6}{3.213}} = 1.93$ s.
$v = \sqrt{2as} = \sqrt{2 \times 3.213 \times 6} = 6.21$ m s$^{-1}$.

slides.heading: Holding a block, pushing it down: the four cases
slides.body_md: The same three forces give every case. Always ask which way the block moves, or **tends** to move, and put friction against it.
bullets: Block **at rest** and tending to slide down (when $\tan\theta > \mu_s$): the least force up the slope to hold it is $mg(\sin\theta - \mu_s\cos\theta)$.
Block that would **not** slide by itself ($\tan\theta < \mu$): to push it **down** at constant speed we need $P = mg(\mu\cos\theta - \sin\theta)$ down the slope.
Friction is large enough to hold a block exactly when $\tan\theta \le \mu_s$.

rows: P = mg(sin θ + μ cos θ)
Held at rest (just stopped from sliding)
P = mg(sin θ − μ cos θ)
a = g(sin θ − μ cos θ)
P = mg(μ cos θ − sin θ), only if tan θ < μ

visual.alt: Table of four situations for a block on a rough slope: pushed up at constant speed, held at rest, sliding freely down and pushed down at constant speed, with the formula and the value for a 25 kilogram block on 35 degrees

slides.narration: The same three forces cover every case. Decide which way the block moves, or tends to move, and put friction against that. If the slope is steep and the block would slide, the least force to hold it up the slope is m g sine theta minus mu cosine theta times m g. If the block would not slide by itself, pushing it down at constant speed needs mu cosine theta minus sine theta times m g.

slides.heading: Pulling or pushing a roller
slides.body_md: A roller of weight $W$ is moved at constant speed by a force $F$ along its handle, at an angle $\varphi$ to the ground. Friction is $f = \mu N$.
bullets: **Pulling:** the vertical part of $F$ points **up**: $N = W - F\sin\varphi$. The normal reaction **falls**, so friction falls.
**Pushing:** the vertical part of $F$ points **down**: $N = W + F\sin\varphi$. The normal reaction **rises**, so friction rises.
Horizontally $F\cos\varphi = \mu N$ in both cases.
For the 50 kg roller, μ = 0.3, φ = 40°: pulling needs 153.3 N, pushing needs 256.5 N.

slides.narration: Look at the free body diagrams. When you pull the roller along its handle, part of the force points upward, so the roller is partly lifted and the normal reaction falls. When you push it, part of the force points downward, so the roller is pressed harder into the ground and the normal reaction rises. Friction follows the normal reaction. For this roller, pulling needs one hundred and fifty three newtons, but pushing needs two hundred and fifty six.

slides.heading: Deriving the pull and the push
slides.body_md: Constant speed: horizontally $F\cos\varphi = \mu N$; vertically the normal reaction follows from the force balance.
bullets: The pull has the **larger denominator**, so it is **smaller**. At $\varphi = 0$ both equal $\mu W$.
The push grows without limit as $\cos\varphi \to \mu\sin\varphi$: a steep handle makes pushing very hard.
The pulling force falls a little at first and is least near an angle whose tangent is $\mu$ (the angle of friction), then rises.

functions.label: pulling: F = μW / (cos φ + μ sin φ)
pushing: F = μW / (cos φ − μ sin φ)

points.label: pull is least near φ = 16.7°: 140.8 N

x.label: handle angle φ above the ground (degrees)

visual.alt: Force along the handle against the handle angle for a 50 kilogram roller with coefficient of friction 0.3: the pulling force dips slightly to 140.8 newtons near 16.7 degrees and then rises to 153.3 newtons at 40 degrees, while the pushing force rises steeply to 256.5 newtons at 40 degrees. The vertical axis starts at 100.
visual.caption: The same angle costs far more when pushing than when pulling.

slides.narration: Write the horizontal and vertical balance. For pulling, F cosine phi equals mu times W minus F sine phi, so F is mu W over cosine phi plus mu sine phi. For pushing the sign changes: F is mu W over cosine phi minus mu sine phi. The pulling denominator is larger, so the pull is smaller. At zero angle both are equal. As the graph shows, the push climbs steeply with the angle.

slides.heading: Angle of friction
slides.body_md: The surface exerts on the block a normal reaction $N$ and a friction $f$. Their resultant $R$ is the **total contact force**. When friction is **limiting**, $R$ makes the largest angle with the normal: the **angle of friction** $\lambda$.
bullets: The **angle of friction** $\lambda$ is the angle between the normal reaction and the resultant of the normal reaction and the limiting friction.
For μs = 0.5 and a 10 kg block: N = 98.0 N, f(max) = 49.0 N, R = 109.6 N and λ = 26.57°.
A larger $\mu_s$ means a larger angle of friction.

slides.narration: The surface pushes on the block with two forces at right angles: the normal reaction and the friction. Their resultant is the total contact force. When friction is at its limit, this resultant is tilted furthest from the normal, by an angle called the angle of friction. The tangent of that angle is the limiting friction over the normal reaction, which is mu s. Here mu s is a half, so the angle is twenty six point six degrees.

slides.heading: Angle of repose, and why it equals the angle of friction
slides.body_md: The **angle of repose** $\alpha$ is the steepest slope at which a body can rest on an inclined plane without sliding down; at $\alpha$ it is just about to slide.
bullets: Because $N$ and $f_{\max}$ together balance the weight, their resultant $R$ is **vertical** and equal to $mg$: the angle between $R$ and $N$ is then the slope angle, so $\lambda = \alpha$.
Measuring $\alpha$ on a tilting plank is a simple way to find $\mu_s$. The result is independent of the mass of the block.
Heaps of sand or grain have an angle of repose, set by the friction between the grains.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: tilting a plank
slides.body_md: A box is placed on a plank which is slowly tilted. In three trials it begins to slip at $27.5^\circ$, $28.0^\circ$ and $28.5^\circ$. Find $\mu_s$ and the angle of friction. Would a box of twice the mass slip at a different angle?
bullets: Mean angle of repose $\alpha = \dfrac{27.5 + 28.0 + 28.5}{3} = 28.0^\circ$.
$\mu_s = \tan\alpha = \tan 28.0^\circ = 0.532$, and the angle of friction $\lambda = \alpha = 28.0^\circ$.
No: $\tan\alpha = \mu_s$ does not contain the mass; both $mg\sin\alpha$ and $\mu_s mg\cos\alpha$ are doubled.

slides.heading: Reducing friction
slides.body_md: In machines and vehicles friction wastes energy and wears parts. We reduce it by these methods.
bullets: **Lubrication:** an oil or grease film separates the surfaces; the friction is that of liquid layers sliding over each other, far smaller than solid on solid.
**Ball bearings and rollers:** rolling replaces sliding, so rolling friction (the smallest kind) applies.
**Streamlining:** a smooth tapering shape lets air or water flow past easily, cutting the fluid drag on vehicles, aircraft and boats.
Where grip is needed we do the opposite: rough tyre treads, shoe soles and sand on icy roads **increase** friction.

slides.narration: In machines and vehicles, friction wastes energy and wears parts away, so we reduce it. Lubrication puts a film of oil or grease between the surfaces, so liquid layers slide instead of solid on solid. Ball bearings replace sliding by rolling, which has far less friction. Streamlining gives vehicles a smooth tapering shape that cuts air or water drag. Where we need grip, we do the opposite and increase friction.

slides.heading: Ball bearings: rolling instead of sliding
slides.body_md: A ball bearing holds a shaft in a fixed housing with steel balls between two rings. When the shaft turns, the balls **roll**.
bullets: The contact between each ball and a ring is rolling contact, so the friction is a small fraction of that of a plain sliding bearing.
Oil or grease inside the bearing lowers the friction further and keeps out dirt.
Heavy loads are carried by many balls at once, and the balls are held apart by a cage so that they do not rub on one another.

slides.narration: To sum up. On a slope the normal reaction is m g cosine theta. Sliding down, the acceleration is g times sine theta minus mu k cosine theta. sections.heading: 1. Views of friction; static, limiting, kinetic and rolling friction
sections.body_md:
- **Friction** opposes the relative motion, or the tendency of relative motion, between surfaces in contact, and acts along them. It is useful (walking, braking) and harmful (wear, heat).
- **Classical view:** the hills and hollows of the two surfaces **interlock**; sliding means lifting over or shearing the hills. It cannot explain why very smooth, clean surfaces can show **more** friction.
- **Modern view:** the surfaces touch only at the tips of the highest hills (real contact area is a tiny fraction of the apparent area). At these points the atoms **adhere** (**cold welding**); friction is the force needed to break the junctions. More pressing flattens more tips, so the real contact area, and so the friction, grows in proportion to $N$.
- **Static friction** is **self-adjusting**: while the body is at rest it equals the applied force (or the balancing component), from zero up to the **limiting friction** $f_{\max}$. For the 35 kg crate: pushes of 60 N and 120 N meet friction of 60 N and 120 N; the limit is 154.3 N.
- **Kinetic (sliding) friction** acts once the surfaces slide; it is nearly constant and **less** than limiting friction (102.9 N for the crate).
- **Rolling friction** acts on a wheel or ball rolling without slipping; no junctions are sheared, so it is **much smaller**: rolling < kinetic < limiting static.

sections.heading: 2. Laws of friction; coefficients; the friction graph; friction is non-conservative
sections.body_md:
- **Laws:** friction acts along the surfaces and opposes the relative motion or its tendency; limiting friction is proportional to the normal reaction, independent of the apparent area of contact, and depends on the nature of the surfaces; kinetic friction is proportional to the normal reaction, nearly independent of speed and area, and smaller than limiting friction.
- **Coefficients** (pure numbers): $\mu_s = f_{\max}/N$ and $\mu_k = f_k/N$, with $\mu_k < \mu_s$; they can exceed 1.
- **Graph of $f$ against $F$:** a straight line of slope 1 (static, $f = F$) up to the peak $f_{\max}$; a drop to $f_k$ when sliding starts; then a nearly horizontal line.
- **Example:** a 3.2 kg block slipping at 12.5 N has $\mu_s = 0.399$; with a 2 kg load the limiting friction becomes 20.3 N. The 35 kg crate pushed with 180 N accelerates at 2.20 m s⁻².
- **Non-conservative:** kinetic friction always opposes the displacement, so the work done is $-\mu_k N \times$ (path length), which depends on the path, and the work around a closed path is not zero. No potential energy exists for friction; the energy becomes heat. Dragging a 20 kg box over a rough floor ($\mu_k = 0.25$): 490 J along 10 m, 686 J along 14 m, 980 J for the round trip.

sections.heading: 3. Motion on a rough incline; pulling and pushing a roller
sections.body_md:
- **Resolve the weight:** $mg\sin\theta$ along the slope, $mg\cos\theta$ perpendicular to it, so $N = mg\cos\theta$ and the greatest friction is $\mu mg\cos\theta$. Friction acts along the slope, against the motion or its tendency.
- **At rest:** $f_s = mg\sin\theta$ (self-adjusting). The block slides when $\tan\theta = \mu_s$.
- **Sliding down:** $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)$; the mass cancels. A block of 25 kg on 35° with $\mu_k = 0.3$ accelerates at 3.213 m s⁻² and, from rest, reaches 6.21 m s⁻¹ after 6 m.
- **Pushed up** with force $P$ along the slope: $P = mg(\sin\theta + \mu\cos\theta) + ma$. For 40 kg on 20° with $\mu = 0.25$: 226.2 N at constant speed, 246.2 N with $a = 0.5$ m s⁻².
- **Held at rest** on a steep slope ($\tan\theta > \mu_s$): least force up the slope $mg(\sin\theta - \mu_s\cos\theta)$. **Pushed down** at constant speed on a slope where $\tan\theta < \mu$: $mg(\mu\cos\theta - \sin\theta)$.
- **Roller** (handle at $\varphi$, constant speed): pulling, $N = W - F\sin\varphi$ and $F = \dfrac{\mu W}{\cos\varphi + \mu\sin\varphi}$; pushing, $N = W + F\sin\varphi$ and $F = \dfrac{\mu W}{\cos\varphi - \mu\sin\varphi}$. Pulling is easier because it **lightens** the roller on the ground and pushing **presses** it down. For 50 kg, $\mu = 0.3$, $\varphi = 40^\circ$: pull 153.3 N, push 256.5 N.

sections.heading: 4. Angle of friction and angle of repose; reducing friction
sections.body_md:
- **Angle of friction** $\lambda$: the angle between the normal reaction $N$ and the resultant $R$ of $N$ and the **limiting** friction. $\tan\lambda = f_{\max}/N = \mu_s$. For $\mu_s = 0.5$, $\lambda = 26.57^\circ$.
- **Angle of repose** $\alpha$: the steepest slope at which a body stays at rest on an inclined plane. At $\alpha$: $mg\sin\alpha = \mu_s N$ and $N = mg\cos\alpha$, so **$\tan\alpha = \mu_s$**. Since $\tan\lambda = \mu_s$ also, **$\alpha = \lambda$**: $N$ and $f_{\max}$ balance the weight, so their resultant is vertical and makes the angle $\alpha$ with the normal. The mass does not matter.
- **Measuring $\mu_s$** with a tilting plank: slips at a mean of 28.0° give $\mu_s = 0.532$.
- **Reducing friction:** **lubrication** (liquid layers slide instead of solid on solid), **ball and roller bearings** (rolling replaces sliding), **streamlining** (smooth tapering shape cuts air or water drag), polishing and wheels. Where grip is wanted (tyre treads, shoe soles), friction is **increased** instead.

notes.exam_tips_md:
- Friction on a body at rest is the balancing force (equal to the push, or to mg sin θ on a slope), not μs N; μs N is the limit.
- Draw the free-body diagram first; friction is along the surface and opposes the motion or its tendency.
- On a slope N = mg cos θ; sliding down a = g(sin θ − μk cos θ); pushed up P = mg(sin θ + μ cos θ) + ma.
- Roller: pulling N = W − F sin φ (easier), pushing N = W + F sin φ (harder).
- tan λ = μs and tan α = μs, so α = λ; show both equations and divide.
- Friction is non-conservative: its work depends on the path and is negative; energy goes to heat.
- State the methods of reducing friction with how each works (lubrication, bearings, streamlining).

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

cards.front_md: What is friction?
cards.back_md: The force opposing the relative motion, or the tendency of relative motion, between two surfaces in contact; it acts along the surfaces.

cards.front_md: State the classical view of the origin of friction.
cards.back_md: The hills and hollows of the two surfaces interlock; sliding means lifting over or shearing the hills.

cards.front_md: State the modern view of the origin of friction.
cards.back_md: The surfaces touch only at a few tips, where the atoms adhere (cold welding); friction is the force to break these junctions.

cards.front_md: Why can very smooth, clean surfaces show greater friction?
cards.back_md: More atoms come into real contact, so adhesion increases; the classical view cannot explain this.

cards.front_md: What does it mean that static friction is self-adjusting?
cards.back_md: While the body is at rest it equals the applied force, from zero up to the limiting value.

cards.front_md: Define limiting friction.
cards.back_md: The maximum value of static friction, reached when the body is just about to slide.

cards.front_md: Compare kinetic and limiting friction.
cards.back_md: Kinetic friction is smaller and nearly constant; limiting friction is the larger peak value.

cards.front_md: Arrange static (limiting), kinetic and rolling friction in increasing order.
cards.back_md: Rolling < kinetic < limiting static friction.

cards.front_md: Why is rolling friction so small?
cards.back_md: No sliding at the point of contact, so no junctions are sheared; only slight flattening of wheel and road.

cards.front_md: Define $\mu_s$ and $\mu_k$.
cards.back_md: $\mu_s = f_{\max}/N$ and $\mu_k = f_k/N$; pure numbers with $\mu_k < \mu_s$.

cards.front_md: Does limiting friction depend on the area of contact?
cards.back_md: No: it depends on the normal reaction and the nature of the surfaces, not on the apparent area.

cards.front_md: State the law connecting limiting friction and normal reaction.
cards.back_md: Limiting friction is proportional to the normal reaction: $f_{\max} = \mu_s N$.

cards.front_md: What happens to $f_{\max}$ when the load on a block is doubled?
cards.back_md: It doubles, since $N$ doubles.

cards.front_md: Describe the graph of friction against applied force.
cards.back_md: A line of slope 1 up to the peak $f_{\max}$, a drop to $f_k$ when sliding starts, then a nearly flat line.

cards.front_md: Can a coefficient of friction exceed 1?
cards.back_md: Yes, for sticky pairs such as rubber on dry concrete; it is a ratio of forces.

cards.front_md: Why is friction a non-conservative force?
cards.back_md: The work it does depends on the path (negative along every part), and around a closed path it is not zero.

cards.front_md: Where does the energy lost to friction go?
cards.back_md: It becomes heat at the surfaces.

cards.front_md: Limiting friction for 35 kg with $\mu_s = 0.45$ ($g = 9.8$)?
What is the normal reaction on a block on a slope of angle $\theta$?
cards.back_md: $N = mg\cos\theta$.

cards.front_md: What is the friction on a block at rest on a slope?
cards.back_md: $mg\sin\theta$ (self-adjusting), as long as it is below $\mu_s mg\cos\theta$.

cards.front_md: Write the acceleration of a block sliding down a rough slope.
cards.back_md: $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)$.

cards.front_md: Write the force along the slope to push a block up at constant speed.
cards.back_md: $P = mg(\sin\theta + \mu\cos\theta)$.

cards.front_md: Why does friction act down the slope when a block is pushed up?
cards.back_md: Friction opposes the motion, which is up the slope.

cards.front_md: Why is it easier to pull a roller than to push it?
cards.back_md: Pulling lifts part of the weight, so $N = W - F\sin\varphi$; pushing presses down, $N = W + F\sin\varphi$.

cards.front_md: Write the force to pull a roller at constant speed.
cards.back_md: $F = \dfrac{\mu W}{\cos\varphi + \mu\sin\varphi}$.

cards.front_md: Define the angle of friction.
cards.back_md: The angle between the normal reaction and the resultant of the normal reaction and limiting friction; $\tan\lambda = \mu_s$.

cards.front_md: Define the angle of repose and relate it to $\mu_s$.
cards.back_md: The steepest slope at which a body stays at rest; $\tan\alpha = \mu_s$.

cards.front_md: How are the angle of friction and the angle of repose related?
cards.back_md: They are equal: $\alpha = \lambda$, as both have tangent $\mu_s$.

cards.front_md: Angle of repose for $\mu_s = 0.532$?
cards.back_md: $\alpha = \arctan 0.532 = 28.0^\circ$.

cards.front_md: Name three ways of reducing friction.
cards.back_md: Lubrication, ball bearings (rolling instead of sliding) and streamlining.

questions.stem_md: Two clean steel blocks are pressed together and one is pulled across the other. According to the modern view of friction, the main origin of the resisting force is

options.text_md: interlocking of the visible grooves over the whole of the apparent area of contact
the gravitational attraction between the two blocks
adhesion (cold welding) at the few points where the surfaces really touch
the electric charge produced by rubbing the blocks together

questions.solution_md: The surfaces touch only at the tips of their highest hills. Under high pressure the atoms there stick together (cold welding), and friction is the force needed to break these junctions. Interlocking over the whole area is the classical picture.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (c)

questions.stem_md: A heavy almirah stands on a floor which can give it a greatest friction of 215 N before it slides. A person pushes it horizontally with 85 N, and the almirah does not move. The friction acting on the almirah is

options.text_md: zero, because the almirah is not moving

questions.solution_md: Static friction adjusts itself to the applied force while the body is at rest, up to the limit of 215 N. The push of 85 N is below the limit, so the friction is 85 N, balancing it.

marking_scheme.step: The almirah is at rest, so friction equals the push: 85 N (a)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: For the same pair of surfaces, which list puts the three kinds of friction in increasing order of size?

options.text_md: limiting static friction, kinetic friction, rolling friction
rolling friction, kinetic friction, limiting static friction
kinetic friction, rolling friction, limiting static friction
rolling friction, limiting static friction, kinetic friction

questions.solution_md: Rolling friction is by far the smallest, kinetic friction is next, and limiting static friction (needed to start the sliding) is the largest.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (b)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A trunk is much easier to move on a hand-cart than to drag over the same floor. The main reason is that rolling friction is smaller than sliding friction because

options.text_md: the normal reaction on a rolling wheel is zero
at a rolling contact the surfaces do not slide, so adhesion junctions are not being sheared
a wheel makes the floor smoother as it turns
a rolling body has less weight than a sliding body

questions.solution_md: The part of a wheel touching the ground is momentarily at rest relative to it. No junctions are torn apart, and only the small loss from the slight flattening of wheel and floor remains.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (b)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: Two metal blocks with extremely clean and highly polished faces cling together far more firmly than the same blocks with moderately rough faces. Which statement explains this best?

options.text_md: Polishing makes the hills and hollows interlock more deeply
Polishing increases the weight of each block
Polishing makes the coefficient of friction exactly zero
Polishing increases the real area of contact, so more atoms adhere across the interface

questions.solution_md: On the modern view friction comes from adhesion at the points of real contact. Smoothing the faces brings more of the surface into atomic contact, so friction can rise. The classical interlocking view would predict the opposite.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (d)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: The coefficient of kinetic friction between two surfaces

options.text_md: has the unit of force, since it is a force divided by a force per area
is a pure number, equal to the kinetic friction divided by the normal reaction
has the unit of force per unit area
is always larger than the coefficient of static friction for the same surfaces

questions.solution_md: μk = fk/N is a ratio of two forces, so it has no unit. For the same pair of surfaces it is smaller, not larger, than μs.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (b)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A block is pushed along a table with a force that is slowly increased. In the graph of friction against applied force the friction suddenly falls at the point where the rising straight line ends. This is because

options.text_md: sliding has begun, and kinetic friction is smaller than limiting friction
the surface of the table suddenly becomes smoother
the normal reaction on the block has decreased
the applied force has been removed

questions.solution_md: The rising line is static friction, equal to the push. At its end the limiting value is reached and the block slides; the friction then drops to the smaller kinetic value μk N.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (a)

questions.stem_md: A block of mass 4 kg needs a horizontal pull of 14 N to start sliding on a table. A second block of mass 4 kg is now placed on top of it. The pull needed to start the pair sliding is
questions.solution_md: The limiting friction is μs N. The extra block doubles N and leaves μs unchanged, so the limiting friction, and the pull to overcome it, is 2 × 14 = 28 N.

marking_scheme.step: N doubles, so the limiting friction doubles to 28 N (b)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A brick has faces of 20 cm × 10 cm, 20 cm × 5 cm and 10 cm × 5 cm. Lying on its largest face on a table, it just begins to slide when pulled horizontally with 18.0 N. The force needed to start it sliding when it lies on its smallest face is
questions.solution_md: The weight, and so the normal reaction, is the same on every face, and limiting friction is independent of the apparent area of contact. The force is therefore unchanged at 18.0 N, although the smallest face has only one quarter of the area of the largest.

marking_scheme.step: Limiting friction does not depend on the area, so the force is still 18.0 N (c)

questions.stem_md: A trolley is dragged over a rough floor at a steady 0.5 m s⁻¹ by a horizontal rope whose tension is 36 N. It is then dragged at a steady 1.5 m s⁻¹ over the same floor. The tension needed is about
questions.solution_md: At a steady speed the tension equals the kinetic friction, μk N. Both μk and N are unchanged, and kinetic friction is nearly independent of speed, so the tension is again about 36 N.

marking_scheme.step: Kinetic friction is nearly independent of speed, so about 36 N (a)

questions.stem_md: A box is dragged slowly over a rough floor from P to Q, first along a straight path and then along a longer curved path. The work done by kinetic friction on the box

options.text_md: is negative in both cases and larger in magnitude along the longer path
is the same along both paths, because the end points are the same
is positive in both cases, because friction helps to stop the box
is zero along the straight path and negative along the curved path

questions.solution_md: Kinetic friction has a constant magnitude and always opposes the displacement, so the work done is minus (μk N × path length). A longer path gives a larger negative work; the work depends on the path, so friction is non-conservative.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (a)

questions.stem_md: A block of mass 8 kg is dragged at constant speed over a horizontal table by a horizontal pull of 23.5 N. Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², the coefficient of kinetic friction is
questions.solution_md: At constant speed the pull equals the kinetic friction, so μk = T/(mg) = 23.5/(8 × 9.8) = 0.300, which is 0.30 to two figures.

questions.stem_md: A block slides down a plank inclined at 30° to the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction between block and plank is 0.2. Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², the acceleration of the block is

options.text_md: 4.9 m s⁻²
6.6 m s⁻²
2.9 m s⁻²
3.2 m s⁻²

answer.model_answer_md: The angle of repose $\alpha$ is the steepest angle of an inclined plane at which a body can rest on it. At this angle the body is just about to slide, so friction is limiting. questions.stem_md: A block slides down a rough inclined plane of angle θ. The coefficient of kinetic friction is μk. Derive an expression for its acceleration and show that it does not depend on the mass of the block.

answer.model_answer_md: Perpendicular to the plane there is no acceleration, so the normal reaction balances the component of the weight: $N = mg\cos\theta$. Kinetic friction $\mu_k N$ acts up the plane, against the motion. Along the plane, Newton’s second law gives $ma = mg\sin\theta - \mu_k mg\cos\theta$. Dividing by $m$, $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)$. The mass cancels, so every block, heavy or light, has the same acceleration.

questions.solution_md: N from the perpendicular balance, then Newton’s second law along the plane.

marking_scheme.step: N = mg cos θ; friction μk N acts up the plane
ma = mg sin θ − μk mg cos θ
a = g(sin θ − μk cos θ), independent of m

questions.stem_md: A block is pushed up a rough inclined plane of angle θ at constant speed by a force P acting along the plane. State the direction of friction and derive an expression for P.

answer.model_answer_md: The block moves up, so friction acts down the plane. Perpendicular to the plane, $N = mg\cos\theta$, so friction is $\mu mg\cos\theta$. At constant speed the forces along the plane balance: $P = mg\sin\theta + \mu mg\cos\theta$, so $P = mg(\sin\theta + \mu\cos\theta)$. The push beats both the weight component and friction.

questions.solution_md: Friction opposes the motion; balance along the plane.

marking_scheme.step: Friction acts down the plane, of size μ N with N = mg cos θ
P = mg sin θ + μ mg cos θ (zero net force)
P = mg(sin θ + μ cos θ)

questions.stem_md: A roller of weight W is pulled at constant speed on level ground by a force F along a handle making an angle φ above the horizontal. The coefficient of friction is μ. Derive an expression for F.

answer.model_answer_md: The pull has an upward vertical part $F\sin\varphi$, so the roller is partly lifted and the normal reaction is reduced to $N = W - F\sin\varphi$. Friction is $\mu N$. At constant speed the horizontal part of the pull equals the friction: $F\cos\varphi = \mu(W - F\sin\varphi)$. Collecting the terms in $F$ and solving gives $F = \dfrac{\mu W}{\cos\varphi + \mu\sin\varphi}$, where $W$ is the weight of the roller.

questions.solution_md: Vertical balance gives N; horizontal balance gives F.

marking_scheme.step: N = W − F sin φ
F cos φ = μ(W − F sin φ)
F = μW / (cos φ + μ sin φ)

questions.stem_md: A roller of weight W is pushed at constant speed on level ground by a force F along a handle making an angle φ with the horizontal. The coefficient of friction is μ. Derive an expression for F and say why it exceeds the force needed to pull it.

answer.model_answer_md: The push has a downward vertical part $F\sin\varphi$, which presses the roller into the ground, so the normal reaction is $N = W + F\sin\varphi$. At constant speed the horizontal part of the push equals the friction: $F\cos\varphi = \mu(W + F\sin\varphi)$, giving $F = \dfrac{\mu W}{\cos\varphi - \mu\sin\varphi}$. The denominator is smaller than in the pulling case, so $F$ is larger, because pushing raises the normal reaction and friction.

questions.solution_md: Same balance as for a pull, with the sign of F sin φ reversed.

marking_scheme.step: N = W + F sin φ for a push
F cos φ = μ(W + F sin φ) gives F = μW / (cos φ − μ sin φ)
Larger than for pulling: N and friction are greater

questions.stem_md: Define the angle of friction and show that the tangent of the angle of friction is equal to the coefficient of static friction.

answer.model_answer_md: The angle of friction $\lambda$ is the angle between the normal reaction $N$ and the resultant $R$ of $N$ and the limiting friction $f_{\max}$. The normal reaction and the friction act at right angles to each other, so they form a right-angled triangle with $R$, and $\tan\lambda = \dfrac{f_{\max}}{N}$. Since the limiting friction is $f_{\max} = \mu_s N$, we get $\tan\lambda = \mu_s$.

questions.solution_md: Right-angled triangle of N, f(max) and R.

marking_scheme.step: λ: angle between N and the resultant R of N and limiting friction
N and f(max) are perpendicular, so tan λ = f(max)/N
f(max) = μs N, so tan λ = μs

questions.stem_md: Describe three methods of reducing friction in machines and vehicles, saying in each case how friction is reduced.

answer.model_answer_md: Lubrication places an oil or grease film between the surfaces, so layers of liquid slide over each other instead of solid on solid. questions.stem_md: (a) Explain the modern view of the origin of friction, and show how it accounts for the proportionality of limiting friction to the normal reaction. [3] (b) With the help of the graph of friction against applied force, explain what is meant by saying that static friction is self-adjusting. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The surfaces touch only at the tips of their highest hills, so the real area of contact is a tiny fraction of the apparent area. At these tips the atoms adhere (cold welding), and friction is the force needed to shear the junctions. A larger normal reaction flattens more tips, so the real contact area grows in proportion to $N$, and so does friction: $f_{\max} = \mu_s N$.

(b) On the graph, for small applied force $F$ the body stays at rest and the friction rises along a straight line with $f = F$, so friction adjusts itself to match the push, from zero up to a peak at the limiting friction. After that the body slides and the friction drops to the kinetic value.

questions.solution_md: Real contact at tips, then the 45° rising line up to the peak.

marking_scheme.step: Surfaces touch only at the tips of the hills; atoms adhere (cold welding)
Friction is the force to shear the junctions
Greater N flattens more tips, so real contact area and friction grow in proportion to N
Static part of the graph: line of slope 1, f = F, up to the limiting friction
Friction adjusts to the push until the limit, then drops to the kinetic value

questions.stem_md: (a) What is meant by a conservative force? Give one reason why friction is not conservative. [2] (b) A 15 kg box is dragged slowly once round a rectangular track of 4 m by 3 m on a rough horizontal floor, μk = 0.2, g = 9.8 m s⁻². Find the work done against friction in one round and the work done by gravity, and state what the results show. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A conservative force does the same work between two points whatever the path, so the work around a closed path is zero. Friction always opposes the displacement, so the work it does is negative and grows with the path length: it depends on the path.

(b) The friction is $\mu_k mg = 0.2 \times 15 \times 9.8 = 29.40$ N and the path length is $2(4 + 3) = 14$ m, so the work done against friction is $29.40 \times 14 = 411.6$ J. The work done by gravity is zero, since the height does not change. The box returns to its starting point yet friction has done work, so friction is non-conservative.

questions.solution_md: Work against friction is f times the whole path; gravity does zero.

marking_scheme.step: Conservative: work independent of path, zero over a closed path
Friction opposes the displacement: the work depends on the path length
f = μk mg = 29.40 N, path 14 m
Work against friction = 411.6 J; work by gravity = 0
Non-zero work over a closed path: friction is non-conservative

Draw a labelled free-body diagram in words, and derive an expression for its acceleration. [3] (b) A 7 kg block is released from rest on a plank inclined at 28° with μk = 0.25. Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², find the time it takes to slide 3 m and its speed then. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The forces on the block are its weight $mg$ acting vertically down, the normal reaction $N$ perpendicular to the plane, and kinetic friction $\mu_k N$ acting up the plane, opposite to the motion. There is no acceleration perpendicular to the plane, so $N = mg\cos\theta$. Along the plane, Newton’s second law gives $ma = mg\sin\theta - \mu_k mg\cos\theta$, hence $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)$, which is independent of the mass.

(b) From the result of (a), $a = 9.8(\sin 28^\circ - 0.25\cos 28^\circ) = 2.438$ m s$^{-2}$. Starting from rest, $s = \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ gives the time for 3 m as $t = \sqrt{2 \times 3/2.438} = 1.57$ s, and the speed at the end is $v = at = 3.82$ m s$^{-1}$.

[3] (b) A 30 kg trolley is pushed up a ramp of 25° with μ = 0.2. Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², find P for constant speed and for an acceleration of 0.4 m s⁻². [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The block moves up the incline, so friction $\mu N$ acts down the incline, against the motion. There is no acceleration perpendicular to the incline, so $N = mg\cos\theta$. Along the incline, Newton’s second law gives $P - mg\sin\theta - \mu mg\cos\theta = ma$, so $P = mg(\sin\theta + \mu\cos\theta) + ma$.

(b) The component of the weight along the ramp is $124.2$ N and the friction is $\mu mg\cos\theta = 53.29$ N. For constant speed the push must equal their sum, $P = 124.2 + 53.29 = 177.5$ N. With an acceleration of 0.4 m s$^{-2}$ the push is larger by $ma$, so $P = 177.5 + 30 \times 0.4 = 189.5$ N.

(a) The angle of friction is the angle between the normal reaction and the resultant of the normal reaction and the limiting friction. The angle of repose is the steepest slope of an inclined plane on which a body can remain at rest.

(b) At the angle of repose $\alpha$ friction is limiting: $mg\sin\alpha = \mu_s N$ and $N = mg\cos\alpha$, so $\tan\alpha = \mu_s$. For the angle of friction $\lambda$, $\tan\lambda = f_{\max}/N = \mu_s$. Both have tangent $\mu_s$, so $\alpha = \lambda$.

questions.stem_md: (a) Explain how (i) lubrication, (ii) ball bearings and (iii) streamlining reduce friction. [3] (b) A shaft carries a load of 800 N. In a plain bearing the effective coefficient of friction is 0.3; with a ball bearing it is 0.006. Find the friction in each case and how many times smaller it becomes. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) Lubrication puts an oil or grease film between the surfaces, so layers of liquid slide over each other instead of solid on solid. (ii) In a ball bearing the balls roll between the rings, so rolling friction replaces sliding friction and is much smaller. (iii) Streamlining gives a smooth tapering shape, so air or water flows past easily and the drag falls.

(b) Plain bearing: $f = \mu N = 0.3 \times 800 = 240.0$ N. Ball bearing: $f = 0.006 \times 800 = 4.80$ N. The friction becomes $240.0/4.80 = 50.0$ times smaller.

questions.solution_md: Fluid film, rolling contact, smooth flow; then f = μN.

marking_scheme.step: Lubrication: a liquid film separates the surfaces, giving liquid friction
Ball bearings: rolling replaces sliding; streamlining: smooth shape lowers the fluid drag
Plain bearing f = 240.0 N; ball bearing f = 4.80 N
